title: Body and soul (CCC 362–365)
hook: the soul is the form of the body; together one person

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Creed's things visible and invisible: heaven and earth, angels, and all that is. Your line was seen and unseen. What unseen thing held you up yesterday? Day one thousand seventy-two.

Dust first, then breath. That's the order in the second chapter of Genesis. God shapes the man out of the ground, a figure lying there, finished and still. Then God breathes into him, and only then does he rise. The Douay-Rheims puts it like this: "And the Lord God formed man of the slime of the earth: and breathed into his face the breath of life, and man became a living soul." Look closely at the last words. The verse doesn't say God slipped a soul inside a body, the way you'd drop batteries into a flashlight. It says the man became a living soul. The whole of him. Today's word is the one that verse ends on.

The Catechism takes this up in a handful of short paragraphs, and it begins by refusing to cut a person in half. A human being, it says, is at once bodily and spiritual. Then it does something quietly surprising with the word soul. In scripture, it notes, soul often simply means a life, or the whole person. When a psalm says my soul thirsts for God, the whole person is thirsty. But soul can also mean what's innermost in someone, what's of greatest value, the part by which a person is most especially made in God's image. The Catechism keeps both meanings. Then it turns to the body. The body, it says, shares in the dignity of being made in the image of God. It isn't a shell, a costume, or a cage the soul is waiting to escape. It's a human body precisely because a spiritual soul gives it life. And then comes the sentence this whole section leans on. The union of soul and body is so deep, the Catechism says, that the soul is to be considered the form of the body. Form, in this older sense, means roughly what makes a thing the living thing it is. So spirit and matter in a person aren't two natures glued together. Their union makes one nature. One person. That has very ordinary consequences in Catholic life. The sacraments come through the body: water poured on a forehead, oil on the hands of the sick, bread placed in a palm. Catholics kneel, stand, make the sign of the cross. And the reverse is true too. A tired body shapes a prayer; a grief settles into the shoulders. In this teaching, that isn't a flaw in the design. It is the design.
screen: `AT ONCE BODILY AND SPIRITUAL.` · `SOUL: A LIFE, OR WHAT'S INNERMOST.` · `THE BODY SHARES GOD'S IMAGE.` · `THE SOUL IS THE FORM OF THE BODY.` · then, large: `ONE PERSON.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: let body and soul take the same two minutes. Settle, and breathe. Start with the body. Feet on the floor. The weight of your hands. Your jaw. Find one tight place and let it loosen a little. Then, without changing anything, notice what's on your mind and heart today: a worry, a person, a hope. Don't sort out which part belongs to the body and which to the soul. Let them be one person, sitting here. If you pray, you can offer the whole of it to God, just as it is. If you don't, stay with the breath going in and out, the breath Genesis began with. The bell holds the time.
Soul. In scripture, often the whole living person; in the Catechism, also the form of the body, so that soul and body make one person. Today's word.
Your line: one person. Today, do one small thing for the body and one for the soul, a glass of water and a minute of quiet, and notice they're both for the same you. Day one thousand seventy-two.

howItsDone: Catholic teaching holds that soul and body form one person, so Catholic worship is bodily: water, oil and bread in the sacraments, and kneeling, standing and the sign of the cross at prayer.

fork.reveal: "and man became a living soul." not a soul dropped in: a whole person, alive.

original.note: the Hebrew word behind "soul" at the end of Genesis 2:7: a living being, all of it.

trapdoor: what you thought: the soul is the invisible you, riding around inside a body.
what it means: in Catholic teaching, soul and body are so united that together they are one person.
what a scholar hears: the Catechism's phrase that the soul is the "form" of the body, a term Catholic theology carries over from philosophy.

notes: CCC 362–365 paraphrased (the Catechism's English text is not public domain): bodily and spiritual (362), two senses of 'soul' (363), the body's dignity (364), soul as 'form' of the body and one nature (365).
'Form here is a word from old philosophy' (Aristotelian-Thomist hylomorphism; Council of Vienne): the Catechism itself does not name the philosophy. Keeper may cut or adjust the gloss.
Original game: נֶפֶשׁ (nefesh) as the Hebrew behind 'soul' in Genesis 2:7 (nefesh chayyah). Confirm pointing.
Psalm reference ('my soul thirsts for God') paraphrased, not quoted.
